newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees flee ethnic fighting in east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Refugees flee ethnic fighting in east Zaire.

text.p: Fighting between Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsi rebels has flared in eastern Zaire, triggering an exodus of tens of thousands of Hutu refugees from nearby camps, relief sources said on Saturday.
Humanitarian sources in the eastern town of Bukavu said at least 28 civilians were killed on Friday in attacks around the village of Kiliba and a sugar factory there.
They said fighting between troops and ethnic Tutsis, known as Banyamulenge, as well as rebel raids on camps housing Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi resumed on Saturday.

In Zurich, the Swiss government said it would not force Zaire's ailing president, Mobutu Sese Seko, to leave if he needed more medical treatment for cancer when a temporary visa expires on October 27.
Swiss television said the 66-year-old ruler would probably move to a villa he owns at Cap Martin in the south of France.
Diplomats fear that Mobutu's prolonged absence will fuel chaos in Zaire and lead to a wider conflict in Central Africa.

"Renewed fighting has broken out this morning between the Banyamulenge and Zairean armed forces near Luvengi refugee camp," Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in Rwanda, said.
"The populations of both Kagunga and Runingo (camps), some 46,000 refugees, have all moved," he told Reuters in Kigali.

Zaire is host to hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees who fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 massacres of minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners there. Other Hutu refugees fled similar ethnic conflict in Burundi.
Some 220,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees languish in 12 camps north of Uvira, a town near Burundi in the delta to the northwest of Lake Tanganyika surrounded by steep hills.
Stromberg said some refugees had gone "to Uvira, some into the hills above Uvira, some into banana plantations, and the remainder have dispersed".
He said Banyamulenge, ethnic Tutsis who came to Zaire from Rwanda in the late 18th century, attacked Kagunga on Friday.
Zaire has been reinforcing and rearming troops in the area.

But Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo this week tried to ease ethnic tension in the east, saying the province's deputy governor overstepped his powers by ordering some 200,000 Banyamulenge Tutsis to leave and had been suspended.
A senior Zairean military commander said Tutsi Banyamulenge from Rwanda's army had crossed the border from Burundi on Friday and had targeted civilians living around Kiliba.
"When they arrived they opened fire with light arms on the local population living in villages around Kiliba," he said.
Aid workers in Bukavu said that dead and wounded from Friday's attacks had been arriving in Uvira.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said a plane carrying doctors aborted a landing at Kiliba on Friday after being fired on.
The Zairean military commander said Kiliba was quiet on Saturday but that Zairean troops were pursuing rebels near Bwegera, about 25 km (16 miles) away.
Some Banyamulenge have lived in Zaire for generations. Zaire accuses the Tutsi-dominated army of Rwanda of training and arming Banyamulenge guerrillas to destabilise the region.
The Banyamulenge say they are fighting for their right to Zairean citizenship. They say they are discriminated against by indigenous Zaireans on the basis of language and ethnicity.
Aid workers in Rwanda quoted sources in Uvira as saying Zairean residents had taken to the streets to demonstrate against the Banyamulenge.
